lessons.title: Set membership and subsets
lessons.summary: Membership asks whether one object belongs to a set; subset asks whether every element belongs.
lessons.body:
Almost every structure in computer science is built from two ideas: a **mathematical set** (a collection of things) and a **mathematical function** (a rule that maps each thing in one set to exactly one thing in another). A simple model treats a type as a set of values and a mathematical relation as a set of tuples. SQL tables can contain duplicate rows, and a hash table usually maps a key through a hash value to a bucket. Getting fluent with the vocabulary pays off everywhere else in this subject.

## Sets

A set is an unordered collection of distinct elements. Curly braces list what is in it, and only membership counts: the order you write the elements in and any repeats make no difference.

Writing the numbers 1, 2 and 3 in a different order, or listing 1 twice, still describes the same three-element set.

These concepts have notation you will see constantly:

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Membership | An object belongs to a set |
| Non-membership | An object does not belong |
| Subset | Every element also belongs to another set |
| Proper subset | A subset that is not equal |
| Empty set | A set with no elements |
| Cardinality | The size of a set |

For example, take a two-element set containing 1 and 2, and a three-element set also containing 3:

```formula essential
1 ∈ A     3 ∉ A
A ⊆ B     A ⊂ B
|A| = 2
where
A: the example set {1, 2}
B: the example set {1, 2, 3}
∈: is an element of
∉: is not an element of
⊆: is a subset of: every element of the left-hand set is also in the right-hand set (the two may be equal)
⊂: is a proper subset of: a subset that is not equal, so the right-hand set has at least one extra element
| |: vertical bars around a set mean its cardinality: the number of elements it has
In words: 1 is in A but 3 is not; everything in A is also in B, and B has an extra element (3), so A is a proper subset of B; A has 2 elements and B has 3.
```

Sets can be written by listing elements, or with **set-builder notation**, which describes the elements by a rule. It resembles a Python comprehension, but mathematical sets can also be infinite:

```formula reference
E = { x ∈ ℤ : 0 ≤ x < 10, x mod 2 = 0 }
where
E: the set being defined (the even numbers below 10)
x: a stand-in for each candidate element
ℤ: the integers: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …
∈: is an element of
{ x ∈ ℤ : … }: set-builder notation: the set of all integers x that make the condition after the colon true. The colon reads "such that"; some books write a vertical bar | instead
≤: is less than or equal to
<: is less than
mod: the remainder after dividing, so x mod 2 = 0 means x is even
In words: A set-builder rule keeps exactly the integers from zero through nine that are even.
```

For example, select even integers from zero through nine in Python, where `%` is the remainder operator:

```python
# Keep exactly the even candidates below 10.
E = {x for x in range(10) if x % 2 == 0}
```

Common number sets: ℕ (natural numbers; whether 0 is included varies by author, so check), ℤ (integers), ℚ (rationals, the fractions of integers) and ℝ (reals, every point on the number line).

> [!warning] Elements versus subsets
> The empty set is a subset of every set, but it is an element of a set only if that set literally lists the empty set inside its braces. The set containing just the empty set has one element; the empty set itself has none.

```formula essential
∅ ⊆ A   for every A
∅ ∈ {∅}     ∅ ∉ {1, 2}
where
∅: the empty set, the set with no elements, also written {}
A: any set at all
⊆: is a subset of: every element of the left-hand set is in the right-hand set
∈: is an element of
∉: is not an element of
{ }: curly braces: the set of the things listed inside
In words: the empty set is a subset of everything (it has no element that could fail to be in A), but it is only an element of a set that lists it, like {∅}. That set has one element; ∅ has none.
```

Sets are unordered and deduplicated. Converting a list to a set and back loses order and duplicates. Python sets only hold hashable elements, so use `frozenset` for a set of sets.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: An empty shopping basket
> An empty basket contains nothing; a basket holding an empty box contains one object.
>
> **How it maps:** Membership asks what is inside the outer collection. A collection holding the empty set has one element even though that element itself contains nothing.
>
> **Where it stops:** Physical baskets have capacity and order, while mathematical sets do not.

## Key takeaways

- Membership asks whether one object belongs to a set; subset asks whether every element belongs.
- The empty set is a subset of every set; a set containing the empty set has one element.

## Further reading

- [Set (mathematics) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics))
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: A set contains exactly the numbers 1 and 2. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The empty set is a subset of it.
options.explanation: There is no element of the empty set that could fail the subset test.

options.text: The empty set is one of its elements.
options.explanation: The only listed elements are the numbers 1 and 2.

options.text: A different set containing only the empty set has one element.
options.explanation: Its one element is itself a set; the outer collection is not empty.

options.text: Listing 2, 1 and 1 describes the same set.
options.explanation: Sets ignore order and duplicate listings.

options.text: The set containing only 1 is one of its elements.
options.explanation: That singleton is a subset, but it is not one of the two number elements.

questions.workedExample: First ask what the elements are: here they are numbers. Membership checks one object against that list. Subset inclusion instead checks every element of a collection. The empty collection has no counterexample to that check. Wrapping it in an outer set creates a collection with one element. Reordering or repeating listed elements never changes membership.

lessons.title: Set operations and De Morgan’s laws
lessons.summary: Union keeps either set; intersection keeps shared elements; symmetric difference keeps exactly one.
lessons.body:
## Set operations

These operations build new sets from old ones. The **universe** U is the set of everything under discussion (all users, all integers), which a complement needs so it knows what "not in A" ranges over.

```formula essential
A ∪ B = { x : x ∈ A or x ∈ B }
A ∩ B = { x : x ∈ A and x ∈ B }
A \ B = { x : x ∈ A and x ∉ B }
A ⊕ B = (A ∪ B) \ (A ∩ B)
Aᶜ = U \ A
where
A, B: any two sets
x: a stand-in for an element
U: the universe: the set of everything under discussion
∪: union: in A or B (or both)
∩: intersection: in both A and B
\: set difference: in A but not in B (some books write A − B)
⊕: symmetric difference: in exactly one of the two sets (some books write A △ B)
ᶜ: complement: everything in the universe U that is not in A
∈: is an element of
∉: is not an element of
{ x : … }: the set of all x that make the condition after the colon true
In words: union keeps anything in either set, intersection keeps what they share, difference keeps A's elements that B lacks, symmetric difference keeps what is in exactly one, and the complement is everything in the universe that is not in A.
```

The picture shows how the three regions of two overlapping sets line up with these operations:

```
+---------+---------+---------+
| A only  |  both   | B only  |
| A \ B   | A ∩ B   | B \ A   |
+---------+---------+---------+
```

For sets containing 1, 2, 3, 4 and 3, 4, 5, the shared elements are 3 and 4. The symmetric difference keeps 1, 2 and 5. With the universe fixed to 1 through 6, the first set’s complement contains 5 and 6.

Python's built-in set supports union, intersection, difference and symmetric difference; complement needs an explicit universe, `U - a`. They are the bread and butter of practical code (deduplicating, finding common users, permission checks):

```python
a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5}
# Set results below ignore display order.
a | b   # {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
a & b   # {3, 4}
a - b   # {1, 2}
a ^ b   # {1, 2, 5}
a <= b  # False: is a a subset of b?
```

**De Morgan’s laws** explain how “not” changes a condition: outside a union means outside both sets, while outside an intersection means outside at least one.

```formula essential
(A ∪ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ
(A ∩ B)ᶜ = Aᶜ ∪ Bᶜ
where
A, B: any two sets inside a universe U
ᶜ: complement: everything in the universe U that is not in the set
∪: union: in either set
∩: intersection: in both sets
In words: "not in (A or B)" is the same as "not in A and not in B", and "not in (A and B)" is the same as "not in A or not in B". The complement flips union into intersection and back.
```

Only 6 is outside both example sets. This tests the meaning of “neither”, without needing separate calculations for both sides.

This is the same rewrite you do when you push a `NOT` through an SQL WHERE clause.

## Key takeaways

- Union keeps either set; intersection keeps shared elements; symmetric difference keeps exactly one.
- Complements depend on a fixed universe, and De Morgan’s laws exchange union and intersection.

## Further reading

- [Set (mathematics) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics))
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt:
What does this print?

```python
a = {1, 2, 3, 4}
b = {3, 4, 5}
# Sort exclusive elements for display.
print(sorted(a ^ b))
```

options.explanation: That is `a & b`, the intersection. `^` is symmetric difference, which keeps elements in exactly one of the sets.
That is `a - b`, the difference. Symmetric difference also keeps 5, which is in b but not a.
That is `a | b`, the union. Symmetric difference removes the shared elements 3 and 4.
Correct. `^` is symmetric difference: elements in a or b but not both. 3 and 4 are in both, so they are dropped.

questions.workedExample: The shared elements are 3 and 4, so symmetric difference removes them. Elements 1 and 2 belong only to the first set, while 5 belongs only to the second. Sorting those survivors prints `[1, 2, 5]`. The code tests membership in exactly one set, not arithmetic XOR of the elements.

questions.prompt: A query filters with `WHERE NOT (country = 'UK' OR plan = 'free')` (assume no NULLs). Which condition selects exactly the same rows?

options.text: `country <> 'UK' AND plan <> 'free'`
options.explanation: Correct. By De Morgan's law, NOT (A OR B) is (NOT A) AND (NOT B). As sets: the complement of the union of UK rows and free rows is the intersection of the non-UK rows and the non-free rows.

options.text: `country <> 'UK' OR plan <> 'free'`
options.explanation: This keeps the OR. De Morgan's law flips OR to AND when you push the NOT inside. This version would include UK users on paid plans.

options.text: `NOT country = 'UK' OR plan = 'free'`
options.explanation: NOT binds tighter than OR, so this is `(country <> 'UK') OR plan = 'free'`, which includes free users, exactly the ones the original excludes.

options.text: `country = 'UK' AND plan = 'free'`
options.explanation: This is the intersection, not the complement of the union. It selects UK free users, who are excluded by the original.

questions.workedExample: The original excludes a row if it is UK or free. A retained row must therefore be both non-UK and non-free. Replacing AND with OR would wrongly keep UK paid rows or non-UK free rows. The no-NULL premise makes this ordinary two-valued reasoning sufficient; SQL UNKNOWN otherwise needs care.

lessons.title: Power sets and bitmask enumeration
lessons.summary: Each element independently belongs or does not belong to a subset.
lessons.body:
## Power sets

The **power set** P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. Its size is a power of two, because each element is independently either in or out of a subset: two choices, made once per element.

```formula essential
|P(A)| = 2^n   when |A| = n
where
A: any finite set; in the example, the set of the three letters a, b and c
P(A): the power set of A: the set whose elements are all the subsets of A
n: the number of elements in A
| |: the cardinality: the number of elements in a set
2^n: n copies of 2 multiplied together
In words: Each extra element doubles the number of subsets: every old subset has a version excluding it and a version including it.
```

That "in or out" view is exactly how programmers enumerate subsets with a **bitmask**: an integer whose binary digits (bits) say which elements are in. Number the elements from 0 upwards; each bit of the mask is 1 when the element with that number is in the subset.

With items a, b and c assigned bit positions from lowest to highest, the binary mask 110 selects b and c. Mask zero selects nothing; the mask with every bit set selects everything.

The loop below visits every mask and decodes it back into a subset:

```python
items = ['a', 'b', 'c']
n = len(items)
# One mask per subset.
for mask in range(1 << n):
    # Low shifted bit selects the item.
    sub = [items[i] for i in range(n)
           if mask >> i & 1]
    print(mask, sub)
```

For 20 items there are about a million subsets; for 40, about a trillion. The displayed loop also decodes every mask by checking every item position.

Each mask requires checking every item position. Doubling the number of masks doubles that part of the work; adding items also lengthens the decoding step.

This assumes each bit check costs one step (a unit-cost model) and ignores the cost of formatting and printing.

The count includes the empty subset and the whole set. To count non-empty subsets, subtract one from the total.

For three elements, the eight subsets include the empty one. Excluding only that subset leaves seven.

## Key takeaways

- Each element independently belongs or does not belong to a subset.
- Enumerating subsets takes exponential time; the shown decoder also checks every bit for every subset.

## Further reading

- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: A system adds one more independent on/off feature flag. Every old configuration remains allowed with the new flag either off or on. What happens to the number of configurations?

options.text: It increases by one.
options.explanation: There is a new choice for every old configuration, not just one extra configuration.

options.text: It stays the same because the flag has only two values.
options.explanation: Two choices create distinct versions of every old configuration.

options.text: It doubles.
options.explanation: Each old configuration has exactly two extensions.

options.text: It doubles only if the all-off configuration is excluded.
options.explanation: The power set includes the empty subset; excluding it changes the counting problem.

questions.workedExample: Pair each old configuration with two new ones: new flag off, and new flag on. Different old configurations cannot produce the same extended configuration, and every new configuration comes from one old configuration. This establishes doubling without calculating a large power.

questions.prompt: A loop visits every five-bit mask and keeps a mask only when `bin(mask).count("1") == 2`. What does the filter select?

options.text: All subsets of the five items.
options.explanation: Masks with other numbers of set bits fail the filter.

options.text: Ordered pairs of distinct items.
options.explanation: A bitmask records membership, not selection order.

options.text: Pairs that can select the same item twice.
options.explanation: One bit cannot represent two copies of its item.

options.text: Exactly the subsets containing two distinct items.
options.explanation: Each set bit selects one position, and the filter requires exactly two.

questions.workedExample: Assign one item to each bit position. A 1 means included and a 0 means excluded. Counting the 1s counts selected items. Swapping the order in which two items were selected would leave the same mask, so this models an unordered pair.

lessons.title: Cartesian products and relational rows
lessons.summary: A Cartesian product contains every ordered combination of input elements.
lessons.body:
The **Cartesian product** A × B is the set of all ordered pairs whose first part comes from A and whose second part comes from B. Every element of A is paired with every element of B, so the sizes multiply:

```formula essential
A × B = { (a, b) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B }
where
A, B: the two sets whose ordered pairs are being formed
a: an element of A
b: an element of B
×: between sets, the Cartesian product; between numbers, ordinary multiplication
( , ): an ordered pair: order matters, so (1, 2) and (2, 1) are different
∈: is an element of
{ : }: the set of all things of the form before the colon that satisfy the condition after it
In words: The Cartesian product contains every ordered pair made by choosing one element from the first set and one from the second.
```

Each column of a mathematical table draws values from its own domain, and a row records one combination in column order.

A mathematical table chooses rows from all allowed combinations of its column domains. It need not contain every combination.

If either input set is empty, there are no ordered pairs, so the Cartesian product is empty.

Real SQL tables go a little beyond this model: they can hold duplicate rows. An SQL CROSS JOIN combines every input-row occurrence with every occurrence on the other side, retaining duplicate multiplicities.

## Key takeaways

- A Cartesian product contains every ordered combination of input elements.
- A mathematical relation selects rows from a Cartesian product; SQL preserves row multiplicities.

## Further reading

- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: A catalogue claims to contain the Cartesian product of its sizes and colours. A new colour is added, but only one size is offered in that colour. Is the claim still correct?

options.text: Yes, because the new colour appears somewhere.
options.explanation: A product requires every pairing, not just coverage of each separate category.

options.text: No, unless that is the only size: every size must pair with the new colour.
options.explanation: All combinations of the two input sets are required.

options.text: No, because a Cartesian product cannot change.
options.explanation: Products can change when their input sets change.

options.text: Yes, because order never matters in a pair.
options.explanation: A product has fixed roles for first and second coordinates; missing pairs remain missing.

questions.workedExample: Take any other size. The pair consisting of that size and the new colour belongs to the product of the declared domains, but is absent from the catalogue. The catalogue may be a relation selecting allowed pairs; it is no longer the full product.

lessons.title: Functions, domains and images
lessons.summary: A total function gives each allowed input exactly one output.
lessons.body:
## Functions

A **mathematical function** assigns to every element of its **domain** exactly one element of its **codomain**. Two conditions: every input has an output, and no input has two outputs.

```formula essential
f : A → B
f(a) ∈ B   for every a ∈ A
where
f: the function's name
A: the domain: the set of allowed inputs
B: the codomain: the set the outputs are declared to lie in
a: any input taken from A
f(a): the single output f gives for input a
→: in "f : A → B", "maps elements of A to elements of B"
∈: is an element of
In words: f takes each element of A and gives back exactly one element of B.
```

There is exactly one function from an empty domain to any codomain: it makes no assignments. A nonempty domain cannot map into an empty codomain.

The **function image** (often called the range) is the set of outputs actually hit. It is contained in the codomain but can leave some declared outputs unused.

For example, doubling integer inputs produces only even integers. If all integers are the codomain, 3 is allowed by that declaration but never reached.

## Key takeaways

- A total function gives each allowed input exactly one output.
- The codomain declares possible outputs; the image contains only outputs actually reached.

## Further reading

- [Set (mathematics) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Set_(mathematics))
- [Bijection, injection and surjection — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijection)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: A total function takes the inputs {1, 2, 3}, declares outputs in {a, b, c}, and sends every input to a. What is its image?

options.text: {a, b, c}
options.explanation: This is the declared codomain, including outputs that the function never reaches.
These are inputs in the domain, rather than outputs.
The image contains exactly the outputs reached by at least one input.

options.text: The empty set
options.explanation: The function does produce an output: every input produces a.

questions.workedExample: Evaluate the function at each of the three allowed inputs. All three outputs are a. A set lists distinct elements, so collecting those outputs gives the singleton set {a}.

lessons.title: Injective, surjective and bijective functions
lessons.summary: Injective functions preserve distinctions; surjective functions cover the codomain; bijections do both.
lessons.body:
Three properties matter:

- **Injective** (one-to-one): different inputs give different outputs.
- **Surjective** (onto): every element of the codomain is hit by some input, so the image equals the codomain.
- **Bijective**: both. Every element of the codomain is hit by exactly one input, so an **inverse function** can undo the mapping.

The domain declares the allowed inputs; the codomain declares the allowed outputs. The reference card expresses these properties and the two-way round trip formally.

```formula reference
f(x) = f(y) ⇒ x = y
∀ b ∈ B, ∃ a ∈ A such that f(a) = b
f^{−1} : B → A
f^{−1}(f(a)) = a   and   f(f^{−1}(b)) = b
where
f: a function from A to B
A: the domain, the set of inputs
B: the codomain, the set outputs lie in
x, y: any two inputs from A
a: an input from A
b: an element of the codomain B
⇒: implies
∀: "for every"
∃: "there exists": at least one such element exists
f^{−1}: the inverse of f, read "f inverse": the function that sends each output back to the one input that produced it. The −1 is a label, not a power: f^{−1} is not 1 / f
∈: is an element of
→: in "f^{−1} : B → A", "maps elements of B to elements of A"
In words: An injection preserves differences between inputs. A surjection reaches every declared output. A bijection does both, so it has an inverse that undoes the mapping in both directions.
```

```
injective    surjective   bijective
not onto     not 1-to-1
a -> 1       a -> 1       a -> 1
b -> 2       b -> 1       b -> 2
c -> 3       c -> 2       c -> 3
     4
```

In the left column nothing maps to 4, so the map is not onto. In the middle, a and b share 1, so it is not one-to-one. The right column is a perfect pairing.

For finite sets, an injection cannot have more inputs than possible outputs; a surjection cannot have fewer inputs than required outputs; and a bijection requires equal sizes.

These are necessary size constraints, not guarantees about a particular mapping: even equally sized sets can be connected by a function that merges inputs.

The first one is the **pigeonhole principle** in disguise: put 5 pigeons in 4 holes and two pigeons must share.

> [!example] Why hash functions collide
> Standard SHA-256 accepts messages shorter than 2⁶⁴ bits and produces one of 2²⁵⁶ outputs. Its finite input domain is still vastly larger than its output space. No function from a larger set to a smaller one can be injective, so collisions must exist. Cryptographic hashes are designed so that *finding* one is infeasible, not so that none exist.

## Codomain changes surjectivity

Whether a function is surjective depends on the declared codomain.

Squaring real numbers reaches exactly the non-negative reals. Declaring all real numbers as the codomain makes it non-surjective; declaring only the non-negative reals makes it surjective. Changing the codomain does not stop a positive and negative input sharing a square.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Tickets and seats
> A seat assignment can give every ticket a different seat while leaving some seats empty. It can also fill every seat while assigning some seats more than once.
>
> **How it maps:** Different seats per ticket models injectivity; every seat used models surjectivity. A perfect one-ticket-per-seat match is bijective.
>
> **Where it stops:** This is only a mapping model: a real venue would reject duplicated seat assignments.

## Key takeaways

- Injective functions preserve distinctions; surjective functions cover the codomain; bijections do both.
- Surjectivity depends on the declared codomain, and a smaller hash output space forces collisions.

## Further reading

- [Bijection, injection and surjection — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijection)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: A function f takes inputs 1, 2 and 3 and has declared outputs a and b. It sends 1 and 3 to a, and 2 to b. Which description is correct?

options.text: Injective but not surjective
options.explanation: It is not injective: f sends both 1 and 3 to a, so two different inputs share an output.

options.text: Surjective but not injective
options.explanation: Correct. Both a and b are hit, so it is onto. But 1 and 3 both map to a, so it is not one-to-one.

options.text: Bijective
options.explanation: A bijection needs both properties, and it would also need the two sets to be the same size. Here they have 3 and 2 elements.

options.text: Not a function, because a is used twice
options.explanation: A function may send several inputs to the same output. What it cannot do is send one input to two outputs, or leave an input unmapped.

questions.workedExample: Every declared output is reached: a by inputs 1 and 3, and b by input 2. That establishes surjectivity. The shared output for distinct inputs 1 and 3 disproves injectivity. A function may merge inputs; it may not assign two outputs to one input.

questions.prompt: A colleague wants a hash function from 64-bit account numbers to 32-bit slot numbers in a table that is guaranteed to have no collisions for any possible input. What is the right response?

options.text: Use a cryptographic hash such as SHA-256 truncated to 32 bits
options.explanation: Truncation cannot remove the pigeonhole limit. A 32-bit output is also too small for cryptographic collision resistance: generic birthday search needs only about 2¹⁶ trials.

options.text: It is impossible: no injective function exists from a 2⁶⁴-element set to a 2³²-element set
options.explanation: Correct. An injection can exist only when the domain is no larger than the codomain. With 2⁶⁴ inputs and 2³² outputs, the pigeonhole principle forces collisions, so the table must handle them.

options.text: Use the ID mod 2³² as the slot
options.explanation: Taking the remainder after dividing by 2³² keeps only the low 32 bits. IDs that differ only in the high bits, like 1 and 2³² + 1, collide.

options.text: It is possible if the function is a bijection
options.explanation: A bijection needs equal-sized sets. 2⁶⁴ is not equal to 2³², so no bijection (or injection) exists.

questions.workedExample: There are more possible account numbers than slot numbers. Distinct inputs therefore cannot all get distinct outputs, regardless of the hash algorithm. A table needs collision handling. Perfect hashing for a fixed selected key set is a different promise from avoiding collisions for every possible 64-bit input.

questions.prompt: A function squares any integer input, including negative integers. Its declared codomain is the natural numbers including zero. Which description is correct?

options.text: Injective, because squaring is one-to-one
options.explanation: On all integers, −3 and 3 both square to 9. Squaring is injective on the non-negative integers, and also on the non-positive integers, but not on all integers.

options.text: Surjective, because every natural number is a square of something
options.explanation: Most natural numbers are not perfect squares. 2, 3, 5, 6, 7 and 8 are never outputs.

options.text: Neither injective nor surjective
options.explanation: Correct. −1 and 1 both square to 1, which breaks injectivity, and 2 has no integer square root, which breaks surjectivity.

options.text: Bijective onto its image, so it has an inverse from the natural numbers to the integers
options.explanation: Restricting the codomain to the image {0, 1, 4, 9, …} makes the function surjective, but it is still not injective (a number and its negative collide), so it cannot be inverted.

questions.workedExample: Negative two and positive two both square to four, so distinct inputs collide. No integer squares to two, which is a declared output, so the function is not onto. Restricting the codomain to the image fixes only surjectivity; it does not separate those colliding inputs.

lessons.title: Composition, function counts and round trips
lessons.summary: Composition runs the right-hand function first; merging reachable inputs loses information.
lessons.body:
### Composition and inverses

**Composition** chains two functions: apply one, then feed its output to the other.

```formula essential
(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x))
where
f: the first function applied, from A to B
g: the second function applied, from B to C
A, B, C: the input, intermediate and final output sets, respectively
x: an input from the domain A of f
∘: composition, read "after": g ∘ f means "g after f"
In words: Composition runs the right-hand function first and feeds its output into the left-hand function. Order can change the result.
```

Adding one then doubling a number can differ from doubling then adding one. Composition therefore depends on order.

Compositions preserve these properties: two injections compose to an injection, two surjections to a surjection, and two bijections to a bijection.

If g ∘ f is injective, then f must be injective (if f merged two inputs, g could not separate them again). If a stage merges two intermediate states actually produced that arose from distinct valid inputs, later deterministic stages cannot recover that distinction without additional information. Non-injectivity only on states the pipeline never reaches need not lose information.

### Counting functions

For finite sets, including empty sets, you can count how many functions of each kind exist. Each input chooses an output; for an injection, each choice must avoid the outputs already used.

```formula reference
N_all = n^m
N_inj = n! / (n − m)!   if m ≤ n
N_inj = 0   if m > n
N_bij = m!   when A = B
where
N_all: the number of functions from A to B
N_inj: the number of injections from A to B
N_bij: the number of bijections from A to itself

A: the domain, with m elements
B: the codomain, with n elements
m: the number of elements in A (the inputs)
n: the number of elements in B (the possible outputs)
n^m: m copies of n multiplied together
!: factorial: k! = k × (k − 1) × … × 2 × 1, with 0! = 1
≤: is less than or equal to
>: is greater than
In words: Counting all functions allows every input to reuse any output. Counting injections forbids reusing an output; counting bijections of a finite set counts its reorderings.
```

For three inputs and four outputs, unrestricted functions allow reuse of outputs. Injections forbid reuse, so their available choices shrink after each assignment.

There is one function on an empty domain: it makes no assignments. The reference count uses the combinatorial convention that zero to the zeroth power is one.

## Functions in real code

The mathematical idea of a function is stricter than a programming "function". A routine whose result depends on changing hidden state may return different results for the same explicit arguments. Including the relevant state in the mathematical input gives a function again; reading an immutable constant does not itself violate determinism. Pure terminating routines fit the simple total-function model and can be easier to test, memoise and parallelise.

Injectivity is essential whenever you need a lossless round trip:

- **Serialisation**: `decode(encode(x)) == x` for every valid x is a requirement that `encode` is injective, and `decode` is its inverse on the image.
- **Base64, UTF-8, gzip**: with a fixed encoder configuration and appropriate valid input domain, lossless round trips require injectivity. Ordinary lossy JPEG and MP3 encoding merge distinct inputs; the JPEG family also includes lossless modes.
- **Primary keys**: projecting each row to its primary-key value uniquely identifies that row. A primary key combines uniqueness with non-nullness; a bare UNIQUE constraint can permit multiple nulls depending on the database and configuration.
- **Permutations in shuffles and ciphers**: a block cipher with a fixed key is a bijection on blocks, otherwise decryption would be ambiguous.

An output side effect can violate purity even when the returned result is deterministic.

## Key takeaways

- Composition runs the right-hand function first; merging reachable inputs loses information.
- Counting total functions chooses an output for every input; lossless round trips require injective encoding.

## Further reading

- [Bijection, injection and surjection — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bijection)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: You enumerate functions from three inputs to four possible outputs. How does requiring injectivity change the choices?

options.text: Each input must choose an output not used by earlier inputs.
options.explanation: This preserves distinctions between inputs.

options.text: Each output must be used at least once.
options.explanation: That is surjectivity and is impossible here with fewer inputs than outputs.

options.text: Only the set of used outputs matters.
options.explanation: Which input receives which output distinguishes functions.

options.text: An input may be left without an output.
options.explanation: A total function still assigns exactly one output to every input.

questions.workedExample: For unrestricted functions an output can be reused. To enumerate injections, track previously chosen outputs and forbid them for later inputs. Choosing three outputs is not enough: assigning those outputs to particular inputs also matters.

questions.prompt: A pipeline applies a function f and feeds its output into a function g. The complete pipeline is injective: distinct original inputs always produce distinct final outputs. Which statements must be true? Select all that apply.

options.text: f is injective
options.explanation: Must be true. If f sent two different inputs to the same place, g would receive the same intermediate value and could not distinguish them.

options.text: g is injective
options.explanation: Not necessarily. The second stage only needs to preserve distinctions among intermediate values actually reached by the first stage; the worked example gives a counterexample.

options.text: f is surjective
options.explanation: Not necessarily. The first stage can leave intermediate values unused while the composition still distinguishes every input.

options.text: For finite input and final output sets, there are at least as many possible final outputs as original inputs.
options.explanation: Must be true. An injection between finite sets needs a separate possible output for each input.

questions.workedExample: If the first stage merged distinct inputs, the second stage would receive exactly the same intermediate value and could not distinguish them. Thus the first stage is injective. The second stage may still merge intermediate values never reached by the first. For example, a singleton input can visit one intermediate value while a second unused intermediate value maps to the same output. The final injection between finite sets also requires at least as many possible outputs as inputs.

questions.prompt: Assume a deterministic encoder and decoder satisfy `decode(encode(x)) == x` for every valid value x. View `encode` as a total mathematical function from Values to Bytes, and `decode` as one from Bytes to Values, where Bytes is an accepted byte-string domain containing every encoded value. What follows?

options.text: encode is a bijection between values and byte strings
options.explanation: It doesn't force surjectivity: accepted byte strings with non-canonical JSON whitespace, for example, need not be produced by the chosen canonical encoder.

options.text: decode is injective
options.explanation: decode can map several byte strings to the same value, for example JSON with different whitespace. Only encode is forced to be injective.

options.text: encode is injective, and decode is surjective onto Values
options.explanation: Correct. If two values encoded to the same bytes, decode would have to return both of them from one input, so encode is injective. Every value x is what decode returns for encode(x), so decode hits everything.

options.text: encode(decode(b)) == b for every byte string b
options.explanation: That is the reverse round trip, and it fails for non-canonical inputs: decoding `{ "a":1 }` and re-encoding may give `{"a":1}`.

questions.workedExample: Suppose two different values encoded to the same bytes. A deterministic decoder could return only one value for those bytes, contradicting the promised round trip. Thus the encoder is injective. Every valid value is reached by decoding its encoding, so the decoder is onto Values. Accepted non-canonical encodings can still decode to the same value, so the reverse round trip need not hold.

lessons.title: Countability and Cantor’s diagonal argument
lessons.summary: A bijection establishes equal cardinality even for infinite sets.
lessons.body:
## Infinite sets have different sizes

For infinite sets, no finite count gives their size, so "same size" is defined by pairing them up: two sets have the same cardinality exactly when there is a bijection between them, so their elements pair off one-to-one with nothing left over on either side. This leads to surprises.

A set is **countable** if it is finite or in bijection with the natural numbers 0, 1, 2, …: its elements can be listed so every particular element is eventually reached. The integers are countable: list them as 0, 1, −1, 2, −2, ….

The list alternates positive and negative integers while moving away from zero. Every particular integer appears after finitely many steps, although the list never finishes.

The rational numbers are countable too, as are all finite strings over a finite alphabet. Therefore **the set of all programs is countable**.

**Cantor's diagonal argument** shows that the set of infinite binary sequences (equivalently, the power set of ℕ, or the real numbers) is **not** countable. Suppose you had a complete list of sequences. Build a new sequence d by flipping the i-th bit of the i-th sequence:

```formula essential
d(i) = 1 − s_i(i)
where
s_i: the i-th infinite 0/1 sequence in the supposedly complete list (s_1 first, s_2 second, …)
s_i(i): bit number i of sequence s_i: the bits on the diagonal
d: the new sequence being built
d(i): bit number i of d
i: a position, 1, 2, 3, …
In words: d takes the diagonal bit of each listed sequence and flips it (1 − 0 = 1, 1 − 1 = 0), so d disagrees with every listed sequence somewhere and cannot be on the list.
```

```
s1 = 0 1 1 0 1 ...
s2 = 1 1 0 0 0 ...
s3 = 0 0 0 1 1 ...
s4 = 1 0 1 1 0 ...
d  = 1 0 1 0 ...   (flip diagonal)
```

The diagonal bits are 0, 1, 0, 1, so the new sequence starts 1, 0, 1, 0. It differs from the first sequence in position one, from the second in position two, and so on. It cannot occur anywhere on the supposed complete list. **Cantor’s theorem** generalises this:

Every set has strictly more subsets than elements: there is no bijection between a set and its power set. This holds for infinite sets too, so there is no largest infinity.

> [!note] Why CS cares
> Programs are countable but the set of functions from ℕ to {0, 1} (all possible yes/no problems) is not. So almost all problems have no program that solves them. The halting problem, covered in the computability module, is a concrete example built with the same diagonal trick.

## Key takeaways

- A bijection establishes equal cardinality even for infinite sets.
- Diagonalisation constructs an infinite binary sequence missing from any proposed list.

## Further reading

- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)
- [Cantor's diagonal argument — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantor%27s_diagonal_argument)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT OpenCourseWare](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/6-042j-mathematics-for-computer-science-spring-2015/)

questions.prompt: Which of these sets is **uncountable**?

options.text: All finite strings over the alphabet {0, 1}
options.explanation: Countable. List them by length, then alphabetically: the empty string, 0, 1, 00, 01, 10, 11, 000, … Every string appears at some finite position.

options.text: All syntactically valid Python programs
options.explanation: Countable. Each program is a finite string over a finite character set, and a subset of a countable set is countable.

options.text: All functions from ℕ to {0, 1}
options.explanation: Correct. These are infinite binary sequences, and Cantor's diagonal argument shows no list can contain them all.

options.text: The rational numbers ℚ
options.explanation: Countable, surprisingly. Fractions can be listed by walking the grid of (numerator, denominator) pairs diagonally, skipping duplicates such as 2/4.

questions.workedExample: Finite strings can be listed by increasing length and then lexicographically. Every particular string eventually appears, so programs, as a subset, are countable too. Rational numbers can also be enumerated. For infinite binary sequences, flip the diagonal bit of each listed sequence: the result disagrees with every entry at its own position. No proposed list can therefore be complete.

lessons.title: Relations and their four properties
lessons.summary: A binary relation chooses ordered pairs and can be represented by a matrix or directed graph.
lessons.body:
A function links each input to exactly one output. A **binary relation** is the looser idea: any collection of links between things. "Follows" on a social network, "depends on" between packages, "is congruent to mod 7" between integers and "happened-before" between events in a distributed system are all relations.

Two special kinds of relation do a huge amount of work in computer science. **Equivalence relations** say when two things count as "the same" and split a set into groups. **Partial orders** say when one thing must come "before" another, and are what a build system or a task scheduler sorts.

## What a relation is

A **binary relation** from a set A to a set B is just a set of ordered pairs: it lists which elements of A are linked to which elements of B. A relation on a single set uses pairs from that set on both sides.

```formula essential
R ⊆ A × B
a R b   means   (a, b) ∈ R
where
R: the relation, written as the set of linked pairs
A, B: the sets the first and second parts of each pair come from
×: Cartesian product: A × B is the set of every ordered pair whose first part is in A and second part is in B
⊆: is a subset of
a: an element of A
b: an element of B
a R b: infix shorthand, read "a is related to b by R"
( , ): an ordered pair: swapping different elements changes the pair
∈: is an element of
In words: a relation is any chosen set of pairs (for a relation on one set A, take B to be A as well). Writing a R b is just a shorter way to say that the pair (a, b) is in the set.
```

For example, "is less than" on {1, 2, 3} is the relation {(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)}: 1 < 2 holds, so (1, 2) is in it, while 2 < 1 fails, so (2, 1) is not.

Three equivalent pictures of the same relation on {1, 2, 3}:

```
pairs:   {(1,1), (1,2), (2,3)}

matrix:      1  2  3
          1  1  1  0
          2  0  0  1
          3  0  0  0

graph:   1 --> 2 --> 3
         plus a self-loop 1 --> 1
```

Every matrix cell chooses whether its ordered pair belongs to the relation. Requiring reflexivity fixes the diagonal to present; the other cells remain free unless another property constrains them.

Adding elements increases the number of possible ordered pairs rapidly. The graph view connects relation properties directly to graph structure.

## The four key properties

For a relation R on a set A:

| Property | Definition |
|---|---|
| Reflexive | every element is related to itself |
| Symmetric | every link has its reverse link |
| Antisymmetric | two distinct elements are never linked both ways |
| Transitive | links chain: two steps imply a direct link |

In symbols, one line per row of the table:

```formula essential
a R a   for every a ∈ A
a R b   ⇒   b R a
a R b and b R a   ⇒   a = b
a R b and b R c   ⇒   a R c
where
R: the relation, a set of pairs from A
A: the set the relation is on
a, b, c: any elements of A (each line must hold for every choice)
a R b: a is related to b, that is, (a, b) is in R
∈: is an element of
⇒: implies: whenever the left side holds, the right side must hold too
In words: reflexive means everything relates to itself; symmetric means links go both ways; antisymmetric means the only way to have links both ways is between an element and itself; transitive means a two-step chain always has a direct link.
```

“Less than or equal to” is reflexive and transitive: a number is at most itself, and two forward comparisons chain. It is not symmetric: 1 is at most 2, but the reverse fails.

In the matrix: reflexive means the diagonal is all 1s, symmetric means the matrix equals its transpose. In the graph: reflexive means a self-loop on every node, symmetric means every edge has a reverse edge, transitive means every two-step path has a shortcut edge.

> [!warning] Antisymmetric is not "not symmetric"
> Antisymmetric only forbids two-way links between *different* elements. Equality (=) is both symmetric and antisymmetric. The relation {(1, 2), (2, 1), (1, 3)} is neither: (1, 2) has a reverse, but (1, 3) doesn't.

Some everyday examples:

- **≤ on integers**: reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive. Not symmetric.
- **< on integers**: not reflexive (irreflexive), antisymmetric (vacuously), transitive.
- **"Is a friend of"**: symmetric, usually not transitive.
- **"Follows" on a social network**: none of the four in general.

## Key takeaways

- A binary relation chooses ordered pairs and can be represented by a matrix or directed graph.
- Reflexivity, symmetry, antisymmetry and transitivity describe different constraints on those pairs.

## Further reading

- [Binary relation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_relation)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: A relation is stored as a matrix: row and column labels are the same elements, and a 1 means the pair is related. What does requiring reflexivity force?

options.text: Every cell must be 1.
options.explanation: Reflexivity constrains only each element’s relationship with itself.

options.text: Only the off-diagonal cells may be 1.
options.explanation: That forbids the self-pairs required by reflexivity.

options.text: Every diagonal cell must be 1; other cells are unconstrained by reflexivity alone.
options.explanation: The diagonal contains exactly the self-pairs.

options.text: Every 1 must have a mirrored 1.
options.explanation: Mirroring is symmetry, a different property.

questions.workedExample: For each element, look at the cell whose row and column both have its label. Reflexivity requires that self-pair. It says nothing about a pair of different elements, so those cells remain free unless another property is imposed.

lessons.title: Equivalence classes, partitions and union-find
lessons.summary: Equivalence relations partition a set into disjoint classes, and every partition defines one.
lessons.body:
## Equivalence relations

A relation that is **reflexive, symmetric and transitive** is an **equivalence relation**. It formalises "the same in the way we care about".

Examples:

- **Modular congruence**: integers are related when they leave the same remainder under one fixed positive modulus.
- **Same connected component** in an undirected graph.
- **Case-insensitive equality** of strings: "Hello" and "HELLO" are equivalent.
- **Same hash bucket**: two keys are related when the same fixed bucket-selection function gives the same bucket.

Integers 17 and 5 both leave remainder 2 when divided by 3, so they are equivalent under congruence modulo 3. More generally, equality of outputs under one fixed function is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

The **equivalence class** of an element is everything equivalent to it:

```formula essential
[a] = { x ∈ A : x ~ a }
where
[a]: the equivalence class of a
a: an element of the set A
A: the set the relation is on
x: a stand-in for each element of A
~: the equivalence relation
∈: is an element of
{ x ∈ A : … }: the set of all x in A that make the condition after the colon true
In words: the class of a collects every element equivalent to a, including a itself.
```

Case-insensitive equality needs a fixed normalisation rule. Likewise, “same hash bucket” means the same final bucket-selection function, not necessarily an equal full hash value.

The crucial theorem: **the equivalence classes partition the set**. Every element is in exactly one class, and two classes are either identical or disjoint.

Modulo 3, the classes collect integers with remainder 0, 1 or 2. Every integer belongs to exactly one, including negative integers under the non-negative remainder convention.

The converse holds too: any partition defines an equivalence relation, “in the same block”. Counting equivalence relations therefore amounts to counting partitions; these counts are called **Bell numbers**. Ordering the blocks or their members does not create a new partition.

### Equivalence relations in code

The **union-find** (disjoint-set) data structure maintains an equivalence relation as you add facts like "a ~ b". Each class is a tree with a representative at the root. Because the relation is transitive, merging two classes is all you ever need to do.

```python
parent = {}

def find(x):
    parent.setdefault(x, x)
    while parent[x] != x:
        # Halve paths to speed later finds.
        parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
        x = parent[x]
    return x

def union(a, b):
    # Join the roots of the two classes.
    parent[find(a)] = find(b)

union('a', 'b'); union('b', 'c')
# a and c now belong to one class.
find('a') == find('c')   # True
```

Union-find tracks components for Kruskal's algorithm and can support type-variable unification. Full type unification also needs to handle type structure and checks such as the occurs check.

Python's own contract relies on this theory. Well-behaved value equality is normally an equivalence relation, but Python does not enforce these laws and NaN is a standard exception. Hashable objects that compare equal must have equal hashes, and their hash must stay stable while used as keys.

> [!warning] "Approximately equal" is not an equivalence
> Calling two numbers equal when they are within a small tolerance of each other breaks transitivity, so it cannot be used to bucket values into consistent groups. The example below shows the chain that fails.

With a strict tolerance of 0.1, 0 is close to 0.08 and 0.08 is close to 0.16, but 0 is not close to 0.16. Chaining “close” judgements therefore need not preserve closeness.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Sorting laundry by colour label
> Assign every garment one fixed colour label and put matching labels together.
>
> **How it maps:** Equality of a fixed label forms equivalence classes. Every item belongs to exactly one class, and merging classes is different from changing individual labels.
>
> **Where it stops:** Informal judgements like “nearly the same colour” need not be transitive, so they do not automatically define the same kind of grouping.

## Key takeaways

- Equivalence relations partition a set into disjoint classes, and every partition defines one.
- Union-find merges classes; tolerance-based equality fails transitivity and cannot define consistent classes.

## Further reading

- [Equivalence relation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equivalence_relation)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: Under congruence mod 4 on the set {0, 1, 2, …, 11}, what is the equivalence class of 7?

options.explanation: An equivalence class contains everything equivalent to 7, not just 7. 3 and 11 leave the same remainder.
That is the set of odd numbers, which is the class of 7 under congruence mod 2, not mod 4.
Correct. 7 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, and the elements with remainder 3 in this range are 3, 7 and 11.
These don't share a remainder: 4 and 8 have remainder 0, 7 has remainder 3.

questions.workedExample: Group the permitted integers by their remainder after division by four. The number seven has remainder three, as do three and eleven. These three belong to one class. Each permitted integer belongs to exactly one remainder class, so the classes partition the domain.

questions.prompt: Which of these are equivalence relations? Select all that apply.

options.text: Two people are related when they were born in the same calendar month.
options.explanation: Yes. It means "same value of the birth-month function", and any relation of the form "same output of some function" is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

options.text: Two real numbers are related when the absolute difference between them is less than one.
options.explanation: No. It is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive: 0 is within 1 of 0.6, and 0.6 is within 1 of 1.2, but 0 and 1.2 differ by 1.2.

options.text: Two vertices of an undirected graph are related when there is a path between them.
options.explanation: Yes. A zero-length path makes it reflexive, reversing a path gives symmetry, joining paths end to end gives a walk, from which cycles can be removed to obtain a path, establishing transitivity. The classes are the connected components.

options.text: A set is related to another set when the first is a subset of the second.
options.explanation: No. The subset relation is not symmetric: {1} is a subset of {1, 2} but not the reverse. It is a partial order.

options.text: Two integers are related when their difference is divisible by seven.
options.explanation: Yes. This is congruence mod 7: any number minus itself is 0, which is divisible by 7; if x minus y is a multiple of 7, so is y minus x; and two multiples of 7 add to a multiple of 7.

questions.workedExample: Check all three laws. Sharing a fixed birth month and sharing a remainder are equality-of-output relations. Undirected connectivity includes a zero-length path, reverses paths and joins paths, so it also forms equivalence classes. Tolerance fails transitivity: 0 is close to 0.6 and 0.6 to 1.2, but the endpoints are not within one. Subset inclusion fails symmetry.

questions.prompt: A tool groups items into nonempty, disjoint blocks covering every item. It declares two items related exactly when they share a block. What follows?

options.text: Every such partition defines exactly one equivalence relation.
options.explanation: Sharing a block is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, and fixes every related pair.

options.text: The tool has chosen only a subset, not a relation.
options.explanation: The blocks together determine which ordered pairs are related.

options.text: Reordering the blocks creates a different relation.
options.explanation: Block order does not change which items share a block.

options.text: All blocks must contain the same number of items.
options.explanation: Equivalence classes can have different sizes.

questions.workedExample: Each item shares its block with itself. Sharing is symmetric. If two pairs share through a middle item, the disjoint-block rule puts all three in the same block. Those are the three equivalence laws. Conversely, the relation’s classes recover exactly the original blocks.

options.text: `==` is not transitive, so it is not an equivalence relation
options.explanation: True. Price(1.000) == Price(1.008) and Price(1.008) == Price(1.016), but Price(1.000) != Price(1.016).

options.text: Two objects that compare equal can have different hashes, so a set may hold both
options.explanation: True. 1.004 and 1.006 are within 0.01, but round to 1.0 and 1.01, giving different hashes. Python checks the hash bucket first, so it never notices they are equal.

options.text: Python raises a TypeError because `__eq__` returns a float
options.explanation: `abs(...) < 0.01` is a bool. Python accepts any `__eq__`; it does not verify the equivalence-relation laws.

options.text: Nothing: rounding in `__hash__` makes it consistent with `__eq__`
options.explanation: Rounding gives fixed buckets, but the tolerance window straddles bucket boundaries. Equal objects must always hash equal, and here they don't.

questions.workedExample: The prices 1.000, 1.008 and 1.016 form a chain of pairwise-near neighbours, but its ends are not equal under the tolerance rule. That breaks transitivity. Separately, 1.004 and 1.006 compare equal but round to different values, so the hash methods disagree and a set can retain both. Use the same fixed, immutable normalised value for equality and hashing; restrict monetary inputs to finite values and handle unsupported types with NotImplemented.

questions.prompt:
On the set {1, 2, 3}, consider this relation, written as its set of related pairs:

```formula essential
R = {(1,1), (2,2), (3,3),
     (1,2), (2,1)}
where
R: the relation: the set of ordered pairs that are related
( , ): an ordered pair: (1,2) means 1 is related to 2
{ }: the set of the things listed inside
In words: every element is related to itself, and 1 and 2 are related in both directions.
```

Which statement is correct?

options.text: R is an equivalence relation with classes {1, 2} and {3}
options.explanation: Correct. It is reflexive (all three self-pairs), symmetric ((1,2) and (2,1)) and transitive, and it groups 1 with 2 and leaves 3 alone.

options.text: R is not transitive, because (1,3) is missing
options.explanation: Transitivity only demands (a,c) when (a,b) and (b,c) are both present. No chain leads from 1 to 3, so (1,3) isn't required.

options.text: R is a partial order
options.explanation: (1,2) and (2,1) link two different elements in both directions, which violates antisymmetry, so it cannot be a partial order.

options.text: R is an equivalence relation with a single class {1, 2, 3}
options.explanation: 3 is related only to itself, so it sits in its own class.

questions.workedExample: All self-pairs are present. The only links between different elements join 1 and 2 in both directions. Chaining those links requires the self-pairs already present; no chain reaches 3 from either of them. Thus the classes are the pair containing 1 and 2, and the singleton containing 3. Two-way links between distinct elements rule out antisymmetry.

lessons.title: Partial orders and Hasse diagrams
lessons.summary: Partial orders allow incomparable pairs; total orders compare every pair.
lessons.body:
## Partial orders

A relation that is **reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive** is a **partial order**. A set with a partial order is a **poset** (partially ordered set). A generic partial order is written with a curly less-than sign:

```formula essential
a ≼ a
a ≼ b and b ≼ a   ⇒   a = b
a ≼ b and b ≼ c   ⇒   a ≼ c
where
≼: a partial order, read "precedes or equals" or "is below or equal to"
a, b, c: any elements of the set
⇒: implies: whenever the left side holds, the right side must too
In words: everything is below or equal to itself, two different things can't each be below the other, and "below" chains.
```

Examples:

- ≤ on numbers.
- ⊆ on the subsets of a set.
- "Divides" on positive integers (see below).
- "Must be built before" on build targets (taking the reflexive closure).
- "Happened-before" on events in a distributed system (Lamport's relation, as a strict order).

Divisibility is a useful example of an order that is not total.

For positive integers, “a divides b” means b is a whole-number multiple of a. Three divides twelve. Neither two nor three divides the other, so not every pair is comparable.

Two elements are incomparable when neither precedes the other. The singleton sets containing 1 and 2 are incomparable under subset inclusion.

If every pair is comparable, it is a **total order** (or linear order), like ≤ on integers or alphabetical order on strings.

A **strict partial order** is irreflexive (nothing relates to itself) and transitive.

Removing all self-pairs turns a partial order into its strict version: strictly before, rather than before-or-equal.

An acyclic direct-dependency graph need not itself be transitive; its positive-length reachability relation is a strict partial order.

### Hasse diagrams

A **Hasse diagram** draws a poset without clutter: leave out self-loops and any edge implied by transitivity, and put larger elements higher. Here is "divides" on the divisors of 12:

```
        12
       /  \
      4    6
      |  /  \
      2      3
       \    /
        \  /
         1
```

Read upwards: 2 divides 4, and 4 divides 12, so a path upwards means "divides". 4 and 6 are incomparable (no upward path joins them), as are 4 and 3.

Useful vocabulary for reading order relationships:

- **Minimal element**: nothing is strictly below it. **Maximal element** means nothing is strictly above it. **Least element** (minimum): below everything; **greatest element** means above everything. A poset can have several minimal elements but at most one least element.
- A **chain in a poset** is a set of pairwise comparable elements. **Antichain**: pairwise incomparable.
- An **upper bound (order theory)** is an element at or above both chosen elements. Their **least upper bound (join)** is below or equal to every upper bound (order theory). The **greatest lower bound (meet)** is defined dually: it lies below both and above or equal to every lower bound (order theory). In the subset order, the join of two sets is their union. Posets where every pair has a join and a meet are **lattices**; state-based CRDTs use a join operation on a join-semilattice of states; operation-based CRDTs use different delivery and commutativity conditions.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Getting dressed
> Socks must precede shoes, but putting on a hat need not be ordered relative to either.
>
> **How it maps:** Dependencies produce a partial order: some pairs are constrained and others incomparable. A full dressing sequence is one linear extension.
>
> **Where it stops:** This ignores duration, shared resources and personal preferences; ordering constraints alone do not solve scheduling with those extra limits.

## Key takeaways

- Partial orders allow incomparable pairs; total orders compare every pair.
- Hasse diagrams remove self-pairs and transitive edges, leaving the immediate ordering constraints.

**Minimal** means nothing else in the set is strictly below it (divides it).

lessons.title: Topological order, comparators and vector clocks
lessons.summary: A topological ordering respects every dependency in a finite DAG.
lessons.body:
### Topological sorting

A **linear extension** of a poset is a total order that respects it: a list of all the elements in which everything strictly below another element comes earlier.

A valid list places every prerequisite before its dependent. Incomparable elements can appear in either order, provided all other dependencies are respected.

For a finite DAG of prerequisite-to-dependent edges, finding one is **topological sorting**, and it exists precisely because there are no cycles (a cycle of distinct vertices conflicts with antisymmetry of reachability, and a self-loop would need a target to come strictly before itself).

```python
from graphlib import TopologicalSorter

# target: its prerequisites
deps = {
    'app': {'lib', 'config'},
    'lib': {'utils'},
    'config': set(),
    'utils': set(),
}
ts = TopologicalSorter(deps)
# Emit prerequisites before their targets.
print(list(ts.static_order()))
# e.g. ['config', 'utils', 'lib', 'app']
```

There are usually many valid orders: for any two incomparable elements, some linear extension puts the first earlier and another puts the second earlier. All choices must still respect the other constraints. Build and dependency tools use dependency ordering when prerequisites form a DAG. Cycle policies vary: pip documents an installation fallback for dependency cycles, so not every such tool rejects them.

> [!example] Vector clocks are a partial order
> In a store that tracks versions with vector clocks, each version carries a list of counters, one for each tracked participant. One version is below another when none of its counters is larger. Two versions where neither is below the other are **concurrent**: incomparable in the partial order. Riak and Dynamo-style stores surface these as siblings for the application to merge.

```formula essential
V ≤ W   means   V_i ≤ W_i   for every i
where
V, W: two vector clocks: lists of counters, one per participant
V_i, W_i: counter number i in V and in W
i: a position in the list, one per participant
≤: on the left, the order on whole clocks; on the right, ordinary "less than or equal to" on two counters
In words: One vector clock is at or behind another only when every corresponding counter is at or behind. If each clock leads on a different counter, they are incomparable.
```

## Pitfalls

- **Inconsistent comparators.** Sorting assumes a total (pre)order. A comparator that isn't transitive (say, rock-paper-scissors, or one that compares floats with NaN) can make sort output depend on the input order, or make Java's `TimSort` throw "Comparison method violates its general contract!".
- **NaN breaks reflexivity.** `float('nan') == float('nan')` is `False`, so IEEE 754 floats are not an equivalence relation under `==`. For ordinary float-NaN lookups, retaining the identical key object permits retrieval even though NaN is not equal to itself; another separately created float NaN does not match it.
- **Assuming a total order where only a partial one exists.** Wall-clock timestamps can tie and need not match causality. Lamport timestamps respect causal order but do not detect concurrency; a process-ID tie-breaker can make them total. Vector clocks can expose concurrency under their model.

## Key takeaways

- A topological ordering respects every dependency in a finite DAG.
- Vector clocks form a partial order; comparator and equality contracts need mathematical consistency.

## Further reading

- [Topological sorting — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_sorting)
- [graphlib — Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/library/graphlib.html)
- [Vector clock — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vector_clock)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

A Dynamo-style store holds three versions of a key with vector clocks (counters for nodes A, B, C), compared with this order:

W = [1, 2, 0]
X = [2, 2, 1]
V ≤ W   means   V_i ≤ W_i   for every i
where

V_i, W_i: counter number i of V and of W

options.explanation: Correct. Each of V and W leads on one counter, so neither is below the other and they are concurrent. X is at least both in every component, so it supersedes them.

options.explanation: Every counter of X is at least the corresponding counter in V and in W, so X is comparable with both and the store can discard V and W.

options.explanation: The component-wise order is only partial; that is the whole point. Incomparable versions reveal concurrent writes that a total order would hide.

lessons.title: Reachability and relation closures
lessons.summary: Transitive closure links pairs joined by positive-length paths, including self-pairs reached by cycles.
lessons.body:
## Closures

Often you have a relation that is "almost" what you want. The **transitive closure** is the smallest transitive relation containing it: it links a to b whenever a chain of one or more links leads from a to b.

A positive-length path counts, even if it returns to its starting vertex. Thus a directed cycle makes its vertices reachable from themselves; an isolated vertex does not acquire a self-link merely through transitive closure.

"Can user A reach user B through follows?" and "does package X depend on Y, directly or indirectly?" are transitive-closure questions.

You can compute reachability with a matrix-based algorithm such as Warshall, or search outward from each vertex using adjacency lists. Sparse graphs can favour the search approach.

```formula reference
T_W = O(n^3)
T_S = O(n × (n + m))
where
T_W: running time of Warshall's algorithm, which works on the adjacency matrix
T_S: running time of a breadth-first or depth-first search (BFS or DFS) from every vertex, using adjacency lists
n: the number of elements (vertices)
m: the number of related pairs (edges)
O( ): big-O: grows no faster than the expression inside, up to a constant factor
In words: A matrix-based closure algorithm has cubic growth in the vertex count. Searching from every vertex can use the smaller edge count of a sparse graph, though actual speed also depends on representation and constants.
```

The growth bounds do not promise a particular wall-clock speedup: constants and memory access patterns matter. SQL can compute reachability with a recursive CTE; cycles require duplicate elimination or another stopping rule.

The empty relation on an empty set is already reflexive, symmetric and transitive. For other sets, the **reflexive closure** adds the diagonal, the **symmetric closure** adds reverse edges. The reflexive, symmetric, transitive closure of any relation is an equivalence relation: it groups vertices into connected components after ignoring any edge directions.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: Connecting journeys
> A route map may show only direct legs, while a journey planner asks which destinations can be reached with changes.
>
> **How it maps:** Direct edges are the original relation; allowing any positive number of legs gives transitive closure. A round trip can make a station reachable from itself.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real journeys have timetables and costs. Plain reachability ignores those extra constraints.

## Key takeaways

- Transitive closure links pairs joined by positive-length paths, including self-pairs reached by cycles.
- Reflexive and symmetric closures add self-links and reverse links respectively.

## Further reading

- [Binary relation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binary_relation)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

lessons.title: Counting rules and complements
lessons.summary: Multiply choices along a sequence; add counts only for disjoint alternatives.
lessons.body:
Counting estimates the size of a search space or test set. Before choosing a method, decide what counts as the same outcome and whether cases overlap.

## The two basic rules

**Product rule.** If a task is a sequence of steps, and the number of choices at each step is fixed for that stage, regardless of the earlier choices, multiply the counts.

**Sum rule.** If a task can be done in one of several *disjoint* ways (no outcome belongs to two of them), add the counts.

A four-digit code allows any digit first. If repeats are forbidden, each later position has one fewer available digit. Codes of different lengths are disjoint cases, so their counts can be added.

> [!example] How big is a brute-force search?
> Each extra independent uniformly chosen character multiplies the number of possible passwords by the alphabet size. An assumed guesses-per-second rate can translate this into a search-time estimate, but it is not a hardware benchmark. Human-chosen passwords need a different probability model.

## Counting at least one

Count the complement: all possibilities minus those with none. Choosing a position for a digit and filling the rest freely overcounts strings containing several digits.

All six-character strings over letters and digits split into two disjoint groups: those containing a digit and those containing none. Subtracting the all-letter group counts each valid string exactly once.

If cases overlap, the sum rule needs inclusion–exclusion or a disjoint reformulation.

## Key takeaways

- Multiply choices along a sequence; add counts only for disjoint alternatives.
- For an “at least one” constraint, subtract the outcomes with none from all outcomes.

## Further reading

- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

questions.prompt: Codes use letters and digits and must contain at least one digit. A developer counts by choosing a digit position, choosing its digit, then freely filling the other positions. What is the flaw?

options.text: It misses all codes with two digits.
options.explanation: Those codes are counted, but more than once.

options.text: It excludes all-letter codes incorrectly.
options.explanation: All-letter codes are exactly the invalid cases.

options.text: A code with several digits is counted once for each possible designated digit.
options.explanation: The selected position is extra information not present in the final code.

options.text: It counts order even though codes are unordered.

lessons.title: Permutations and circular arrangements
lessons.summary: Permutations count ordered selections without replacement.
lessons.body:
## Permutations: order matters

A **permutation** is an ordering. Choose the first item, then one of the remaining items, and keep going. Multiplying those shrinking choices gives the **factorial** count:

```formula essential
n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1   for n ≥ 1
0! = 1
where
n: the number of distinct items being put in order, a whole number 0 or more
!: factorial: multiply every whole number from n down to 1. By convention 0! = 1 (there is exactly one way to order nothing)
…: and so on: the pattern continues through every whole number in between
≥: is greater than or equal to
In words: A factorial counts orderings of distinct items: choose the first item, then a remaining item, and keep going. There is one ordering of no items.
```

For an ordered selection filling only some positions, stop choosing when those positions are filled. No item may be reused; asking for more distinct items than exist is impossible.

```formula reference
P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)!
where
P(n, k): the number of permutations of k items from n: ordered selections with no item used twice
n: the number of distinct items available
k: how many places are filled, from 0 up to n
!: factorial: the product of every whole number from that number down to 1, with 0! = 1
In words: An ordered selection without repeats chooses a new item for each successive position. Stop after filling the requested number of positions.
```

Each extra item creates more possible insertion positions. This makes factorial growth eventually exceed every fixed-base exponential, explaining why enumerating all orders quickly becomes impractical.

That is why brute-forcing the travelling salesman problem (trying every ordering of cities) quickly becomes impractical as the number of cities grows (the cutoff depends on the implementation and hardware).

A comparison sort must distinguish every possible ordering of distinct items. Each yes/no comparison supplies at most one binary decision, which gives the familiar worst-case lower bound of linear-times-logarithmic comparisons.

## Circular arrangements

When rotations count as the same seating, divide out the rotational overcounting.

Fix one person’s position and arrange the others relative to them. This removes rotational duplicates. A reflection reverses clockwise order and remains distinct unless the problem explicitly identifies mirror images; with at least three distinct people, identifying reflections halves the count again.

## Key takeaways

- Permutations count ordered selections without replacement.
- Circular seatings of distinct people identify rotations; identifying reflections requires a further adjustment.

## Further reading

- [Permutation — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permutation)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)
