Each exponent bit therefore needs only a bounded number of modular multiplications. Reducing keeps residues bounded by the modulus, but timing still depends on implementation and operand size.

lessons.title: Fermat, Euler and the totient
lessons.summary: Fermat reduces exponents for prime moduli and nonzero residues; Euler generalises to coprime inputs.
lessons.body:
## Fermat and Euler

**Fermat’s little theorem** applies when the modulus is prime and does not divide the base. Raising that base to one less than the prime gives remainder one. These assumptions are essential; a zero residue has positive powers that remain zero.

```formula reference
a^{p − 1} ≡ 1 (mod p)
where
a: an integer that p does not divide
p: a prime number
≡: is congruent to: leaves the same remainder after dividing by p
mod: "modulo": remainders after dividing by p
In words: For a prime modulus and a base not divisible by that prime, raising the base to one less than the prime gives remainder one. Whole blocks of that exponent can therefore be removed.
```

That block of multiplications contributes the multiplicative identity, so removing whole blocks from a non-negative exponent preserves the remainder.

For modulus thirteen, multiplying by twelve more copies of a coprime base leaves the same remainder as before. A shorter cycle may also exist; the theorem guarantees a working period, not always the shortest one.

**Euler’s totient** counts integers from one through a positive modulus that are coprime to it. **Euler’s theorem** says that for a modulus greater than one and a coprime base, raising the base to that count gives remainder one.

```formula reference
φ(p) = p − 1
φ(p × q) = (p − 1) × (q − 1)
a^{φ(n)} ≡ 1 (mod n)   when gcd(a, n) = 1
where
φ(n): phi of n, Euler's totient: how many integers from 1 to n have gcd 1 with n
p, q: distinct primes
n: an integer modulus at least 2; the totient itself is also defined at 1 and equals 1 there
a: an integer coprime to n (sharing no factor with it)
gcd(a, n): the greatest common divisor of a and n
≡: is congruent to: leaves the same remainder after dividing by n
mod: "modulo": remainders after dividing by n
In words: The totient counts integers coprime to a positive modulus. For a modulus greater than one, any coprime base raised to the totient leaves remainder one; special counting rules apply to primes and products of distinct primes.
```

The integers one, three, seven and nine are exactly those from one through ten coprime to ten, so ten’s totient is four. For a prime, every smaller positive integer is coprime, making the totient one less than the prime. This recovers Fermat’s theorem.

> [!warning] Fermat's test can be fooled
> The converse of Fermat's theorem is false: passing the test does not prove a number prime. 561 is a **Carmichael number**: composite, yet it passes Fermat's test for every base that shares no factor with it (see below). Miller–Rabin adds stronger checks; base 2 rejects 561, but a single round is not guaranteed to reject every Carmichael number.

The number 561 factors as three times eleven times seventeen. It is composite despite passing the Fermat test for every coprime base. A test result can satisfy a necessary condition without establishing primality.

## Key takeaways

- Fermat reduces exponents for prime moduli and nonzero residues; Euler generalises to coprime inputs.
- Passing Fermat’s congruence does not prove primality; Carmichael numbers are counterexamples.

## Further reading

- [Modular arithmetic — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modular_arithmetic)
- [Miller–Rabin primality test — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miller%E2%80%93Rabin_primality_test)
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)

lessons.title: RSA construction, correctness and security limits
lessons.summary: The private exponent reverses the public exponent modulo the totient in this construction.
lessons.body:
## RSA

Now everything fits together.

**Key generation**

1. For this mathematical two-prime construction, pick two distinct odd primes. Production key sizes and generation requirements must follow the chosen library and current deployment policy.
2. Multiply the primes to get the public modulus. Its totient is the product of one less than each prime.
3. Choose a public exponent of at least 3, below the modulus, that shares no factor with the totient. The conventional choice is 65537 when it satisfies these requirements; the small example below uses 17.
4. Compute the private exponent: the inverse of the public exponent modulo the totient, with the extended Euclidean algorithm.
5. Public key: the modulus and the public exponent. Private key: the private exponent (and the two primes, kept secret).

A message representative is an integer from zero up to, but not including, the modulus. The following reference records the construction:

```formula reference
n = p × q
φ(n) = (p − 1) × (q − 1)
gcd(e, φ(n)) = 1
d = e^{−1} mod φ(n)
c = m^e mod n
m = c^d mod n
where
p, q: two distinct secret primes
n: the public modulus
φ(n): Euler's totient of n
e: the public exponent, 3 ≤ e < n, often 65537 (not Euler's number 2.718)
d: the private exponent, the inverse of e modulo φ(n)
e^{−1}: the inverse of e: the number that multiplies e to give remainder 1
m: the message representative, an integer with 0 ≤ m < n
c: the ciphertext
gcd: greatest common divisor
mod: "modulo": the remainder after dividing by the number after it
In words: In this two-prime construction, the private exponent inverts the public exponent modulo the totient. Encryption and decryption raise the message representative and ciphertext to their respective exponents modulo the public modulus.
```

**Why it works:**

For a message coprime to the modulus, raising it by a whole totient’s worth of exponent gives remainder one. The public and private exponents multiply to one more than a multiple of the totient, so their composition leaves one copy of the message.

The case where the message shares a factor with the modulus also works. Modulo either prime, a message divisible by that prime remains zero through encryption and decryption. Otherwise Fermat’s theorem applies: the product of exponents is one more than a multiple of that prime minus one. The decrypted residue therefore equals the original residue modulo each prime. Since the two primes are coprime, the Chinese remainder theorem makes the result equal modulo their product as well.

With tiny primes 61 and 53, the public modulus is 3233. Public exponent 17 pairs with private exponent 2753 in this construction. Message 65 encrypts to 2790 and decrypts back to 65. These toy values demonstrate a round trip; they provide no security.

**Security connection:** knowing the secret prime factors lets an attacker compute a private exponent. Inverting RSA has not been proved equivalent to factoring, and attacks can instead target encoding, key generation, side channels or protocols. A sufficiently capable fault-tolerant quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could factor the modulus.

> [!note] Evidence gap
> No universal RSA latency or hardware attack-time estimate is supplied: this lesson has no reproducible benchmark or deployment threat model for one.

> [!warning] Textbook RSA is not secure RSA
> The raw modular-power operation is deterministic (the same message always encrypts the same way) and malleable (multiplying ciphertexts multiplies message representatives modulo the public modulus). Use a vetted library with OAEP for encryption or PSS for signatures and a cryptographically secure random source. Never implement RSA yourself for production use.

Implementations use the **Chinese remainder theorem** to decrypt: compute modulo each prime separately (with half-size numbers) and combine, which reduces operand sizes and can accelerate decryption; the speedup depends on arithmetic, hardware and implementation. Finite-field Diffie–Hellman uses modular exponentiation. Recovering its shared secret from public group elements is the computational Diffie–Hellman problem; solving discrete logarithms would solve it, but the two hardness assumptions are not known to be equivalent. Authentication and the full protocol introduce additional requirements.

## Key takeaways

- The private exponent reverses the public exponent modulo the totient in this construction.
- Raw RSA is deterministic and malleable; secure schemes need encoding, randomness and implementation protections.

## Further reading

- [RSA (cryptosystem) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RSA_(cryptosystem))
- [Mathematics for Computer Science — MIT](https://courses.csail.mit.edu/6.042/spring18/mcs.pdf)
- [PKCS #1: RSA Cryptography Specifications — RFC 8017](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017.html)

options.text: The inverse must be taken modulo the totient in this construction, because it is the exponents’ cycle that must be undone.
options.explanation: The message arithmetic uses the public modulus; the exponent condition uses the totient.

options.text: RSA decryption should multiply the ciphertext by the public exponent.
options.explanation: Decryption uses modular exponentiation, not ordinary multiplication.

options.text: The public exponent must be secret.
options.explanation: It is deliberately part of the public key.

options.explanation: Inverses are defined relative to a particular modulus and need not satisfy another modulus’s condition.

The totient construction enforces this by choosing an inverse modulo the totient. An inverse modulo the public modulus solves a different problem. Correct arithmetic alone still does not make unpadded RSA secure.

questions.prompt: Which statements about **textbook** RSA (the raw formula, with no padding) are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: It is deterministic: encrypting the same message twice gives the same ciphertext
options.explanation: True. There is no randomness, so an eavesdropper can test guesses like "yes" or "no" by encrypting them with the public key.

options.text: It is malleable: from two ciphertexts an attacker can make a valid encryption of the product of their messages
options.explanation: True. The raw RSA primitive is multiplicative modulo the public modulus. OAEP encoding and validation prevent treating arbitrary products of ciphertexts as valid encryptions of corresponding application-message products; they do not change the primitive's algebra.

options.text: Anyone who factors the public modulus can compute a valid private exponent
options.explanation: True. The two prime factors determine the totient. The extended Euclidean algorithm then gives an inverse of the public exponent modulo that totient.

options.text: The private exponent is the inverse of the public exponent modulo the public modulus
options.explanation: False. The private exponent inverts the public one modulo the totient (or the Carmichael function), not modulo the public modulus. That's what makes Euler's theorem cancel the exponent.

options.text: Using the public exponent 65537 is insecure because it is public and small
options.explanation: 65537 is a conventional public exponent and is not inherently insecure. Security also needs valid key generation, a suitable scheme and correct implementation; padding is not the only possible failure point.

questions.workedExample: Raw RSA uses a deterministic modular power, so equal representatives give equal ciphertexts. Its multiplication rule lets ciphertext products represent message products modulo the public modulus. Knowing the prime factors reveals the totient and permits a valid private exponent to be computed. That inverse concerns the exponent cycle, not the public modulus. A conventional public exponent does not fix the encoding weaknesses: use a vetted library with OAEP for encryption or PSS for signatures.
